paper_title: VeriSpoof: Beyond Real or Fake with One Audio LLM

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A speech deepfake detector estimates whether a recording is synthetic, but a forensic analyst also asks which system produced it, whether recordings share a source, and what evidence supports each conclusion. We present VeriSpoof, an audio language model that unifies five tasks with shared weights: deepfake detection, generator attribution (generator, acoustic model and vocoder), recording-condition analysis, synthesized-span localisation, and source verification. Each decision is supported by grounded rationales whose statements can be independently verified. Answers are scored by sentence likelihood, allowing detection and source verification to be thresholded without separate heads. Rationale statements can be checked against waveform measurements, span labels, or generator metadata. Counterfactual examples train decisions to follow the stated evidence. Across the 14 Speech-DF-Arena test sets, VeriSpoof-Plus achieves 2.14% pooled EER, ranking third of 28 systems and first among open-weight systems. VeriSpoof-Base, trained only on official training splits of eight corpora, achieves 4.43% EER, less than half that of the next open-weight detector. With the same weights, VeriSpoof-Plus verifies whether recordings from generators unseen in training share a source at 6.2% EER. Controlled studies show that the audio representation governs detection, the LLM governs recording comparison, and source supervision is necessary for neural-codec fakes. Statement-checkable rationales catch partial fakes missed by one-step answers (99.6% vs. 78.4% on PartialEdit) and determine decisions under edits unseen in training (99.5%). Training updates only 29.7M of 2.85B parameters, fitting a single 24 GB GPU with gradient checkpointing. We release both models, inference code, a demo, and VeriSpoof-Bench, the evaluation suite covering these questions.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Speech deepfakes pose significant security threat nowadays. suspicious speech recording can raise several related questions: whether it is synthetic, which system produced it, and whether another recording came from the same source. Consider voice message submitted as evidence. deepfake detector can tell an analyst that it is probably synthetic, but the analysts next questions are harder: which system produced it, whether it came from the same system as another message in the case, and on what grounds the detector believes so. The answers link recording to tool, and through the tool to person or campaign; conclusion that cannot be explained cannot be contested. 1 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report Figure 1. VeriSpoof at glance. (a) Detection on the 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena [1], pooled EER (one threshold over all sets, the boards ranking); the public snapshot of 31 Oct 2026 with both VeriSpoof models inserted, top 11 shown. (b) The same weights decide whether two spoofed recordings come from the same generator, against pair probe on the frozen anti-spoofing encoder DF-Arena-1B (6.2). (c) Accuracy of the one-step answer and of the decision VeriSpoof-Base reaches after writing its rationale (6.7). (d) Share of decisions that follow localization replaced by its opposite, in wording never used in training (6.8).

Source attribution, verification, and explanation have also been studied. For forensic workflow, open detectors leave three problems. 1. One score answers one question. Source tracing assigns recording to closed set of known systems or attributes [4, 5], while comparing two recordings needs separate Siamese network [6, 7]. Each further question costs another model, trained on its own data. 2. Explanations cannot serve as evidence. Audio language models (ALMs) for deepfakes add explanations [810], but these are free text written or distilled by teacher model. Whether stated observation is true of the recording is not checked, and whether the decision depends on it is not tested. Such an explanation can be fluent and wrong, or correct and irrelevant to the decision [11, 12]. 3. It is unclear where to invest. Speech-recognition encoders have been argued to discard the artifacts of synthesis [13], and source labels are often assumed to help detection [8] without controlling for the number of authenticity labels or training steps. Which part of an ALM limits detection, and which limits comparing recordings, has not been measured. VeriSpoof addresses all three problems in single model: it unifies detection, attribution, recordingcondition analysis, localisation and source verification, and accompanies every decision with rationales that can be checked statement by statement against the signal. For the first, it casts every forensic question as question with candidate answers written as sentences and reads the likelihood of each answer as score, so one model detects spoofs, names the generator, its acoustic model and vocoder, describes the recording channel and verifies whether two recordings share source (Figure 3). For the second, it writes rationales in fixed fields, each with target computed from the exact audio the model hears, so that every statement has check without trusting the model. Training on counterfactual rationales further ensures that the decision follows the stated evidence (Figure 2). For the third, we run controlled studies that change one component or one form of supervision at time on the same test trials, measuring which part of the model limits detection and which limits source comparison. Key results Best open-weight detector. On the 14 Speech-DF-Arena sets, VeriSpoof-Plus reaches 2.14% pooled and 1.79% mean EER (third of 28 systems on the public snapshot), and VeriSpoof-Base, trained on 0.38 utterances of official training splits, 4.43%; the best other open-weight system reaches 9.52% (6.1). The same weights verify sources. For pairs from generators unseen in training, VeriSpoof-Plus decides whether they share source at 6.2% EER for new models of known architectures and 15.0% for new architectures, against 26.5 and 24.8% for pair probe on frozen anti-spoofing encoder; general audio LLMs answer near chance (6.2). Representation decides detection, the LLM decides comparison. With the encoder fixed, how its features are used lowers ASVspoof 5 EER from 9.6 to 3.1% while source verification stays at 1619%; swapping the LLM moves detection by 0.5 points and source verification by 5.5 (6.3). Source labels are necessary for neural-codec fakes. At matched number of authenticity labels, source supervision helps on 8 of 16 sets and hurts on one; with five times more authenticity labels instead, CodecFake+ EER stays at 12.6 against 2.2% (6.5). Checkable, useful and faithful rationales. Statements are checked one by one (SNR and level correct for 88100% of recordings); the decision after reasoning catches partial and unfamiliar fakes the one-step answer misses (99.6 vs. 78.4% on PartialEdit); and with counterfactual training it follows reworded, inverted localization in 99.5% of cases, against 73.8% without (6.66.8). Light to train and run. Only 29.7 of the 2.85 parameters are trained. With gradient checkpointing, every training stage fits single 24 GB GPU, and we estimate that training fits 12 GB GPU and inference an 8 GB GPU (6.9). 3 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report Figure 2. One score versus checkable evidence on the same recording, in which one word of genuine speech was replaced by synthesized speech. Asked directly, the model judges the recording genuine (left). Asked to reason, VeriSpoof-Base states observations, synthesized span and source profile before deciding (right). Each statement is checked against waveform measurement or label ( holds, fails, no label), and replacing the stated span by none flips the decision. Statements are abridged; the full output is in Figure 11. Both models are released: VeriSpoof-Base, trained on the official training splits of eight corpora, and VeriSpoof-Plus, which extends Base with twelve additional corpora and larger balanced training mixture (4), together with the inference code with vLLM [14] backend and hosted demo. We also release VeriSpoof-Bench, the evaluation suite of this report: 54 test subsets with 177,852 items covering detection, attribution, source verification, recording conditions, grounded reasoning, and faithfulness, with scoring scripts and the per-item outputs of both models.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Speech deepfake detection. Most detectors pair self-supervised front-end with light back-end [1517]. Recent work improves generalization through spectral residuals [18], high-order feature interactions [19], stylelinguistics mismatch [20], dedicated pre-training [13], or data composition at scale [2, 3]. Evaluation has moved from ASVspoof [21, 22] and In-the-Wild [23] to multi-set boards such as Speech-DF-Arena [1] and SpoofRadar [24]. These systems return one score per recording; VeriSpoof returns its detection score as the likelihood of its own answer and is evaluated on both boards. Source tracing and verification. Source tracing assigns recording to known system or to attributes such as its acoustic model and vocoder [4, 5], on corpora with many generators such as MLAAD [25] and SpoofCeleb [26]. Dedicated Siamese or two-branch networks score whether two recordings come from the same generator [6, 7]. We pose this comparison to the model that also detects and explains, on open-set protocols with unseen generators or architectures. Audio language models for deepfakes. HoliAntiSpoof unifies detection, method recognition and localization [8], ThinkOmni generates reasoning with localization [9], and ICLAD prompts an ALM with comparison examples [10]. However, general-purpose ALMs [2730] are not trained for these tasks. Their rationales, where present, are free text from teacher model and are not checked against the signal: ICLAD reports hallucinated explanations, and ThinkOmnis training rationales are written by model shown the labels. SpeakerLLM [31] unifies speaker profiling, recording conditions and verification reasoning for speakers. 4 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report Figure 3. VeriSpoof. (1) An 8 waveform, or two for pair, enters (2) the Qwen3-ASR encoder, frozen apart from DoRA adapters. (3) Two learned mixes over its 25 layers feed (4) the audio tokenizer, which pools the recording into 16 utterance tokens and stacks pairs of frames with text time marker every 0.8 s. (5) The prompt places the tokens of A, then those of B, before the question; (6) the frozen LLM with LoRA reads it and (7) returns score, the log-likelihood difference of two answer sentences, rationale whose decision comes last, or per-token synthetic-speech profile. Grey: frozen; dark blue: trained by us, with the stages that train each part (PA: perception alignment, QT: forensic question tuning, RT: grounded rationale tuning). Faithful explanations. In NLP, an explanation is faithful when the decision depends on it, which is tested by editing the rationale and observing the decision [11, 12, 32]. We apply such tests to audio, with edit forms held out from training, and train for them with counterfactual rationales.

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Formulation: Forensic Questions as Answer Scoring
sections.content: Let denote the input, either single recording or pair (x, x), and question with set of candidate answers Aq each written as sentences. An ALM with parameters θ assigns each answer Aq, the likelihood pθ(a u, q) of its tokens. For binary yesno question, let a+ and denote the positive and negative answers; we read the score, sq(u) = log pθ(a+ u, q) log pθ(a u, q). (1) which can be evaluated by equal error rate (EER) and thresholded at chosen false-alarm rate. Questions with more answers are scored by the accuracy of the most likely one. VeriSpoof answers four families of questions (Figure 5): authenticity; attribution of the generator, acoustic model or vocoder; recording condition (noise, reverberation, codec, post-processing); and source verification on pairs (same generator, acoustic model or vocoder?). No question has its own output head. For detection, for example, the question is Is this recording genuine human speech or spoofed speech? Options: bona fide; spoof. and the two answers are full sentences (This recording is spoof: it is synthetic or converted speech, not genuine human speech.); the released models label recording spoofed when sq(x) > 0. Figure 10 shows the template of every question with an example answer. Source verification is not the same as comparing attributes: two recordings from different systems can share every attribute class (e.g., generator family, acoustic model and vocoder), so model that answers same source whenever the attributes agree fails on such pairs. Source-verification test sets therefore balance three strata: SAME, REVERSAL (different systems, every attribute class shared) and DIFF, so that attribute agreement alone does not reveal the answer. sections.title: 3.2 Model
sections.content: Perception in two resolutions. Qwen3-ASR encoder [33] reads an 8 window of the recording. learned weighted sum of the hidden states of all 25 of its layers is passed to an audio tokenizer with two outputs: 16 utterance tokens, which carry what is constant across the recording and serve attribution and verification, and 52 frame tokens of 0.16 s, which preserve temporal information. Time markers every 0.8 are inserted between frame tokens as text, so that the LLM can state spans in seconds. The encoder is adapted with DoRA [34] (r=16) during the first training stage only and frozen afterwards. For pair, the tokens of both recordings are concatenated in the prompt. LLM and read-out. The LLM is MiniCPM5-2B [35, 36], adapted with LoRA [37] (r=16, α=32) on the attention projections. The model has 2.85 parameters, of which 29.7 are trained (6.9). The model is trained with next-token prediction on the answer tokens and answers are scored by Eq. (1). Two auxiliary losses support perception: one-class authenticity loss [OC-softmax; 38] on the pooled audio tokens, which pulls bona fide speech towards learned centre, and per-token head that classifies each frame token as genuine or synthesized from the LLMs hidden state. The per-token head gives synthetic-speech profile over time at no extra cost and serves as reference for how much localization information the hidden states carry (6.6). The model has two output modes: one-step answer scored by Eq. (1), and rationale followed by decision, described in 3.3.

sections.title: 3.3 Rationales written from what the model hears
sections.content: For forensic use, decision must come with evidence that can be verified and contested, so VeriSpoof explains its decisions with rationales whose every statement can be checked independently of the model. rationale = (r1, . . . , rk; d) is sequence of statements in fixed fields followed by decision d. Each statement type τ has checker cτ (x, ri) {true, false} that does not involve the model: OBSERVATIONS (bandwidth class, SNR, speech level, clipping, digital silence) are checked against measurements on the waveform; CHANNEL_STATUS (noise, reverberation, codec) against the logged recording condition; LOCALIZATION (synthesized spans in seconds, or none) against labelled spans; SOURCE_PROFILE (generation method, acoustic modelling, waveform generation) against generator metadata. rationale is grounded if every statement has checker, so its correctness can be measured statement by statement. Channel statements describe the recording, not its authenticity, and are declared non-evidential. The data loader computes them directly from the exact window the model receives after augmentation: it measures observations on the waveform, takes channel statements from the augmentation log, maps labelled spans to window time, and reads the source profile from generator metadata. Each target is therefore true of its input, and the decision, written last, follows from the localization: recording is labeled spoofed if and only if at least one synthesized span is stated, and genuine otherwise. The decision is the final generated token sequence after the rationale fields; it is read as score by Eq. (1) when thresholding is needed, or taken as the generated text directly. Verification rationales have the fields CHANNEL_STATUS, FINGERPRINT, PROFILE_COMPATIBILITY and DECISION; they state the fingerprint verdict before comparing attributes, because the attribute comparison can mislead the decision on REVERSAL pairs (6.7). Figure 11 shows one output of each kind in the Appendix.

sections.title: 3.4 Three training stages
sections.content: Training has three stages, each with its own trainable parts  (Table 19)  . 1. Perception alignment (PA) trains the tokenizer and the encoders DoRA adaptors on detection and source questions with the LLM frozen, so that the audio representation itself learns the relevant information before the LLM can compensate for weak audio tokens. The representation study of 6.3 6 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report is run at this stage for the same reason. 2. Forensic question tuning (QT) adds LoRA on the LLM and trains it on all perception questions, form of multi-task instruction tuning: acoustic model, vocoder, source profile, recording condition, and pair questions on generator, acoustic model, vocoder and the authenticity of both recordings. 3. Grounded rationale tuning (RT) introduces detection and verification rationales and counterfactual examples at lower learning rate. To preserve the one-step answering ability acquired in QT, the question-answering tasks of QT are replayed throughout this stage. Each question has several paraphrases. Two models share this recipe and differ in their training data (4): VeriSpoof-Base, the model of all controlled studies, and VeriSpoof-Plus. Counterfactual examples and their training procedure are described in 3.5.

sections.title: 3.5 Counterfactual training
sections.content: Counterfactual training is applied in stage 3 (grounded rationale tuning). Grounded rationales alone do not make the decision depend on the rationale: the model can decide from the audio and write matching rationale beside it. To make the decision follow the rationale, in 20% of the rationale examples we give the model rationale whose localization is reversed (a labelled span replaced by none, or none replaced by span) and train only the decision that follows. The model is never taught to state something false about the audio. It is taught that the decision must follow the localization it is given. We further test faithfulness with interventions: statement ri is replaced by ri and the model decides again. The decision is faithful if it follows an edited localization (no synthesized segment genuine) and remains the same when an edited non-evidential statement is edited. Besides the edit form used in training, we test held-out forms: paraphrased localization, an inserted span, and contradicted channel or observation statements.

sections.title: 3.6 Inference
sections.content: One-step answers are scored by the likelihood of each candidate answer sentence; rationales are generated greedily. The released package exposes detection (detect), rationales with the per-token profile (explain), source verification at the generator, acoustic-model or vocoder level (same_source), verification rationales (compare), and closed questions on recording conditions and on generators from list the user supplies. vLLM [14] backend generates rationales from the same prompt embeddings (6.9).

sections.title: 4 Training data and recipe
sections.content: Figure 4 summarizes the training data of both models. VeriSpoof-Base. Base uses the official training splits of eight detection corpora, ASVspoof 2019 LA [21], ASVspoof 5 [22], SpoofCeleb [26], MLAAD [25], STOPA [5], DFADD [39], LibriSeVoc [40] and CodecFake+ [41], and the partially spoofed corpora PartialSpoof [42], HAD [43] and PartialEdit [44] for rationales: about 0.38 utterances. No evaluation split of any corpus is used. Base serves every controlled study of this report, so that its results are not tied to particular choice of extra data. VeriSpoof-Plus. Plus keeps the recipe and adds twelve corpora, spoofed speech from ASVspoof 2015 [45], ADD 2022 train / dev [46], Fake-or-Real [normalized version; 47], ReplayDF [48], SpeechFake [49], WaveFake [50] and Codecfake [codec conditions F01F06; 51], and bona fide speech from Common Voice 15.0 subset [52], LibriSpeech [53], AISHELL-3 [54], GigaSpeech [55] and CN-Celeb2 [56], 4.0 utterances more. Its spoofed half is balanced over 211 sources (one generator of one corpus; MLAAD generators grouped into 82 architecture families) and its bona fide half over 18 datasets, so that the large added corpora do not dominate. 7 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report Figure 4. Training data. VeriSpoof-Plus keeps everything VeriSpoof-Base is trained on and adds twelve more corpora, balanced over 211 spoof sources and 18 bona fide datasets. Grey: corpora with spoofed speech; purple: partial spoofs whose labelled spans train the rationales; blue: bona fide speech only. Bottom: training steps of the three stages, perception alignment (PA), forensic question tuning (QT) and grounded rationale tuning (RT), to scale. Held-out generators. The MLAAD generators of the unseen-model and unseen-architecture verification protocols are removed from all training data, including four SpeechFake systems that are among them (ChatTTS, FireRedTTS, Parler-TTS, StyleTTS 2). Codecfake and CodecFake+ are different corpora: CodecFake+ has codec re-synthesis part (CodecFake+ in our tables) and part generated by codec-based speech generators (CoSG), whose generators are unseen in training. Augmentation. Training copies carry labelled noise MUSAN [57], reverberation and codecs, including narrowband codecs, drawn anew for every example because the encoder runs inside the training loop. The recording-condition questions and the CHANNEL_STATUS statements are trained on these labels. Post-processing (silence trimming or padding, gain with clipping, highor band-pass filtering) is applied identically to both classes, without naming it in the answer, which removes channel shortcuts (6.4); on the corpora added for Plus, augmentation is applied without naming it either. Recipe. Base trains 8k / 20k / 10k steps in the three stages at global batch of 32 on one 48 GB GPU, about 14 GPU-hours (6.9). Plus runs perception alignment for six balanced epochs (79.2k steps) at global batch of 64 on two GPUs and keeps the step counts of the other two stages. Learning rates fall from 104 in perception alignment to 2105 (LoRA) in rationale tuning. Questions are sampled by task weights; the full settings are in Table 19 and the training data in Figure 4. 8 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report

sections.title: 5 Evaluation suite
sections.content: Public detection boards. For detection we score every line of the 14 official protocols of Speech-DFArena [1]: ASVspoof 2019 LA (LA19), 2021 LA and DF (LA21, DF21) [58], ASVspoof 5 (ASV5), In-the-Wild (ITW) [23], Fake-or-Real (FoR), Codecfake (Codec), ADD 2022 tracks 1 and 3 (A22T1, A22T3), ADD 2023 rounds 1 and 2 (A23R1, A23R2) [59], DFADD, LibriSeVoc (LSV) and SONAR, 2.34 trials in total. We report the pooled EER, which uses one threshold over all sets and decides the board ranking, and the mean over sets, and compare with the boards public snapshot of 31 Oct 2026. We also score the 16 sets of the SpoofRadar v1.0 protocol [24], which adds XMAD-Bench [60] in seven languages and SpoofCeleb, with its pooled metrics  (Table 17)  . We did not submit to either leaderboard; our numbers are computed with the boards own protocol files. VeriSpoof-Bench. The other questions have no public benchmark, so we built one and release VeriSpoofBench. It has 54 subsets with 177,852 items in six groups (Figure 5, Figure 9): up to 10,000 items per closed-answer subset, drawn once and used for every model and checkpoint, so differences between columns of table are paired. Source verification on MLAAD is split by how far the generators of pair are from training: seen generators, unseen models of seen architecture, and unseen architectures. Degraded copies come in two kinds: aug. copies apply noise, reverberation and codecs drawn as in training, and cond. copies carry one logged condition per recording, against which channel statements are checked. Rationales are evaluated on 500 utterances per set, and verification rationales on pairs balanced over the SAME, REVERSAL and DIFF strata. +proc marks copies with post-processing. Metrics. Yesno questions are scored by EER on the score of Eq. (1); questions with more answers by the accuracy of the most likely option. Observation statements are correct when the stated class matches the measured one (SNR within 10 dB, speech level within 5 dB, bandwidth and clipping classes). Localization is scored by the IoU of stated and labelled spans, and the per-token head by F1 of the synthesized class on the 0.16 grid. Faithfulness is the share of decisions that follow an edited localization (follow rate) or stay unchanged under an edited non-evidential statement (stay rate). Baselines. Detection is compared with the open-weight systems of Speech-DF-Arena and SpoofRadar; proprietary systems, whose training data are undisclosed, are listed for reference. No open system answers the source questions, so we train pair probe on the frozen anti-spoofing encoder DF-Arena-1B with the Base training data, and prompt six general audio LLMs zero-shot with closed answer options [2830, 6163]. Controls. Controlled comparisons change one factor at time with all else fixed and use the same test trials. The supervision study (6.5) fixes its decision rule before the results and reports paired, class-stratified bootstrap intervals.

sections.title: 6.1 Detection on public benchmarks
sections.content: Best open-weight detector. On the 14 Speech-DF-Arena sets  (Table 1)  , VeriSpoof-Plus has the lowest mean EER (1.79%) and pooled EER (2.14%) of all open-weight systems; the next best, DF-Arena-1B, reaches 5.66% and 9.52%, and every other open-weight system, including four listed only on SpoofRadar, has mean EER above 5%. Inserted into the public snapshot, Plus ranks third of 28 systems by pooled EER, behind two proprietary systems, and Base fourth (Figure 1a). Base is trained on the official training splits of eight corpora; Fake-or-Real, Codecfake, ADD and SONAR have no training data in Base, and their EERs are its main gap to the systems above it. The score is the likelihood of the models own answer, so answering in sentences costs neither detection head nor accuracy. SpoofRadar and unseen languages. sections.title: 6.2 Source verification and attribution
sections.content: The same weights verify sources. For two recordings from generators unseen in training  (Table 4)  , VeriSpoof-Plus verifies shared source at 6.17% EER when the generators are new models of known architectures and at 15.00% when the architectures are new, which suggests that source cues are tied to architectures. It names seen generators (96.8%) and recording conditions (81.3%). Degraded copies remain hard (2330% EER), as noise and codecs mask the detail that separates generators. The pair probe on the frozen DF-Arena-1B encoder reaches only 24.829.0% EER on the MLAAD sets; Base is better on every MLAAD, SpoofCeleb and degraded set and worse on STOPA (20.88 vs. 17.9) and ASVspoof 5 (23.27 vs. 22.2), and Plus is better on every set. General audio LLMs cannot answer these questions. Prompted with the same closed options on 1,000 items per set  (Table 5)  , six general audio LLMs answer the same-source and recording-condition questions near chance (48.453.3 and 16.422.6% balanced accuracy on average). On authenticity they reach 52.164.7%; the best, Qwen3-Omni, reaches 76.090.2% on the ASVspoof sets but stays near chance on SpoofCeleb, LibriSeVoc and both CodecFake+ sets. On the same items Base and Plus reach 95.9 and 96.5% on authenticity, 77.9 and 82.8% on same source, and 76.9 and 83.0% on recording condition. More generators sharpen the fingerprint. Plus improves source verification on 10 of 11 sets  (Table 6)  , by 67 points on degraded copies (unseen models 13.80 6.17%): seeing more generators sharpens the notion of source fingerprint. It loses on SpoofCeleb (11.25 12.20) and on naming the acoustic model under an unseen vocoder (84.7 69.8%), the two tasks that rest on SpoofCelebs labels, whose share of the training data is far smaller in Plus. sections.title: 6.4 Channel shortcuts
sections.content: Without post-processing in training, the model reads channel properties as evidence  (Table 9)  : 2 kHz high-pass makes 11.626.8% of spoofs pass as genuine, and 0.5 of digital silence or +10 dB gain with clipping makes 12.4 and 15.6% of genuine ASVspoof 5 speech look spoofed. Applying the same post-processing to both classes reduces these to 1.78.4%. Labelling the post-processing in the answer gives no consistent further gain (1.98.9%), so what removes the shortcut is that both classes share the channel, not that the model is told about it; we keep the unlabelled form. Gain with clipping remains the largest error (8.4%).

sections.title: 6.7 Reasoning versus the one-step answer
sections.content: Reasoning catches what the one-step answer misses. The decision after reasoning agrees with the one-step answer on 97.699.6% of whole-utterance spoofs of known corpora, and where they disagree the reasoning is usually right (Figure 8a, Table 13): 99.6 vs. 78.4% on PartialEdit, 97.4 vs. 85.8% on unseen MLAAD generators. The one-step answer summarizes the whole recording, whereas writing the localization first makes the model inspect it frame by frame. Unlike the chain-of-thought of ThinkOmni, which lowered accuracy [9], our intermediate steps are perception targets with checks. For Plus the one-step answer is near chance on HAD (48.4%) and 80.0% on PartialSpoof, while its reasoning decision reaches 97.6 and 89.2%: the data added for Plus shift the one-step answer on partial fakes, but writing the localization first still finds the edited span. On whole-utterance sets the one-step answer of Plus catches up (MLAAD 99.4%), and the two agree on 98.499.6%. Reasoning is therefore most useful where the training data of the one-step answer do not cover the fake. In practice, the one-step score suits screening at scale, and rationale suits the recordings an analyst has to decide on. The order of statements matters. Comparing attributes before the verdict led verification rationales to answer same source whenever attributes matched, failing on REVERSAL pairs (accuracy 0.31) although the one-step answer was good  (Table 14)  ; in two rationale-tuning runs that differ only in field order, stating the fingerprint verdict first raised this to 0.67. sections.title: 6.8 The decision follows the stated evidence
sections.content: Without counterfactual training, the model told that no segment was synthesized still answered spoof for 42% of unseen MLAAD recordings (Figure 8b); with it, the decision follows the edit on every set. This carries over to edits never seen in training (Figure 8c): paraphrased opposite localization is followed in 99.5% of cases (73.8% without counterfactual training), an inserted span in 100%, and the decision stays unchanged in 100% when channel or observation statements are contradicted. The decision thus depends on the localization, which is the statement that should carry it, and not on the statements declared non-evidential. The model is never trained on false statement about the audio, and the statement accuracies of Table 11 are those of the model trained with counterfactual examples.

sections.title: 6.9 Compute: training and running on small GPUs
sections.content: Only 1% of the parameters are trained. VeriSpoof trains 29.7 of its 2.85 parameters: the audio tokenizer (17.85 M, all stages), the encoder DoRA adapters (3.24 M, perception alignment), the LLM LoRA adapters (8.60 M, question and rationale tuning) and the per-token head (6 k); one-class head of 0.53 is used in training only. The encoder and the LLM stay frozen in bf16 and hold no gradients or optimizer state, so the training state of the adapters (fp32 copy, gradients and Adam moments) takes about 0.5 GB. Memory is set by the frozen weights, about 5.3 GiB in bf16, and by activations. 20 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report Training. Table 15 gives the peak memory logged in our runs on one 48 GB L40S. The released Base was trained without gradient checkpointing, which peaks at 2145 GiB and takes about 14 GPU-hours for the three stages (logged throughput 50, 24 and 18 examples per second). With gradient checkpointing, runs of the same model and stages at the same micro-batch of 32 peak at 1117 GiB, so the full recipe, global batch included, fits single 24 GB GPU such as an RTX 3090 or 4090, at lower speed. Activations grow with the micro-batch, about 0.170.34 GiB per example; we estimate that micro-batch of 8 with gradient checkpointing, accumulated to the same global batch, needs 79 GiB per stage, within 12 GB GPU, and micro-batch of 12 approaches the 5.3 GiB of frozen weights. Offloading the frozen weights to CPU memory, for example with DeepSpeed ZeRO-Offload, would lower the floor further at the cost of speed. These settings change the micro-batch only, not the recipe; we have not trained at them. sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Speech forensics can be cast as scored question answering with grounded and faithful rationales. VeriSpoof reads every answer as score, writes rationales whose statements can be checked against the signal, and is trained so that its decision follows the evidence it states. With one set of weights it is the best open-weight detector on Speech-DF-Arena and SpoofRadar, verifies the source of recordings from unseen generators, attributes generators and describes recording channels. Controlled studies show where to invest: the representation and how it is trained decide what is detected, the LLM decides how well recordings are compared and how evidence is worded, and supervision that distinguishes how audio was produced adds what more binary labels cannot, at least for neural-codec fakes. Its rationales catch 21 VeriSpoof: beyond real or fake with one audio LLM Technical Report partial fakes that one score misses and determine the decision even under edits never seen in training. We release both models, the inference code and demo, and the evaluation protocol for the questions beyond detection.

SOURCE_PROFILE: The generation method cannot be determined. DECISION: The recording is spoof: synthetic segments are embedded in genuine speech. Checks: bandwidth fails (measured full band); SNR and level hold; span IoU 0.64; decision correct. Verification rationale, STOPA REVERSAL pair (different systems, every attribute class shared) CHANNEL_STATUS: The first recording has no audible noise, no noticeable reverberation and Opus compression; the second recording has no audible noise, no noticeable reverberation and no codec compression. FINGERPRINT: The latent source-fingerprint cues show clear differences. PROFILE_COMPATIBILITY: Generation method is similar (both copy-synthesis of real speech). Acoustic modelling is similar (both copy-synthesis without an acoustic model). Waveform generation differs (time-domain neural-codec decoders vs GAN vocoders). DECISION: Channel degradations are present, but they are not evidence about the generation source. Across the source profile, the attributes are mixed. This agrees with the fingerprint cues. Taken together, the recordings come from different generation systems. Checks: decision correct; the attribute statements fail (both systems are diffusion / flow-matching TTS with GAN vocoders), which the check exposes while the fingerprint verdict carries the decision.
